content: 1. Poliovirus Excretion and Surveillance: Data on poliovirus excretion, including vaccine-associated paralytic poliomyelitis (VAPP) and immunodeficiency-related vaccine-derived poliovirus (iVDPV), is analyzed by sentinel facilities, countries, and years. This includes mapping cases of primary immunodeficiency (PID) patients excreting poliovirus by geographic area, country, and year. The age and sex distribution of PID patients with prolonged Sabin strain or iVDPV excretion is also studied, along with the duration of viral shedding (prolonged versus chronic) and the type of PID diagnosis. 2. Investigation and Treatment: The percentage of PID patients with prolonged Sabin or iVDPV excretion who underwent detailed investigations, including contact tracing and community assessments, is recorded. Results from environmental and contact sampling to investigate iVDPV cases are also analyzed. Additionally, the percentage of PID patients receiving antiviral treatment and those who cleared poliovirus excretion post-treatment is monitored. 3. Outcomes and Monitoring: Outcomes of cases, such as continued shedding, cessation of shedding, death, or loss to follow-up, are documented. Surveillance for poliovirus excretion among PID patients is reviewed quarterly in conjunction with other polio surveillance systems, such as acute flaccid paralysis (AFP) and environmental surveillance (ES). Data is analyzed annually for country risk assessments and reports to national certification committees for polio eradication. 4. Performance Indicators for PID Surveillance: Key performance indicators include: Testing over 90% of registered PID patients for poliovirus excretion. Conducting detailed case investigations within 48 hours for over 80% of PID patients with poliovirus excretion. Ensuring over 80% of specimens arrive at WHO-accredited laboratories in good condition and within three days of collection. Providing laboratory results to submitting agencies within defined timeframes (e.g., 14 days for poliovirus isolation). 5. Poliomyelitis Epidemiology: The Global Polio Eradication Initiative (GPEI) was launched in 1988 to eradicate polio by 2000. At that time, over 350,000 cases of paralytic poliomyelitis were reported annually across 125 countries. The last case of wild poliovirus type 2 (WPV2) was reported in 1999, and WPV3 in 2012. WPV2 and WPV3 were certified eradicated in 2015 and 2019, respectively. As of October 2022, WPV1 remains endemic in Afghanistan and Pakistan. The global spread of poliovirus has been a public health emergency of international concern (PHEIC) since 2014. 6. Poliovirus Characteristics and Transmission: Polioviruses are non-enveloped RNA viruses of the Picornaviridae family, with three serotypes (types 1, 2, and 3). They are resistant to many disinfectants but are inactivated by ultraviolet light. Transmission occurs via fecal-oral and oral-oral routes, with mixed patterns depending on sanitation levels. 7. Vaccines: Oral Polio Vaccine (OPV): Since 2016, bivalent OPV (bOPV) containing Sabin strains types 1 and 3 is used in routine immunization. Monovalent OPVs are used for outbreak responses. Novel OPVs (nOPVs) with enhanced genetic stability are under development. Inactivated Polio Vaccine (IPV): IPV is administered via injection and contains all three poliovirus serotypes. It is available as a standalone vaccine or in combination with other antigens. 8. Vaccine-Derived Polioviruses (VDPVs): These rare strains arise from genetic mutations in the live attenuated vaccine virus in OPV. VDPVs are classified into: Circulating VDPVs (cVDPVs): Occur in under-immunized populations, where the virus mutates and regains neurovirulence. Immunodeficiency-related VDPVs (iVDPVs): Observed in individuals with immune deficiencies who cannot clear the vaccine virus. Ambiguous VDPVs (aVDPVs): Isolates that do not fit into the other categories. 9. Clinical Aspects of Poliomyelitis: Most poliovirus infections are asymptomatic, but approximately 25% develop minor symptoms like fever, headache, and sore throat. A small percentage may experience aseptic meningitis. Paralytic polio occurs in less than 1% of infections, leading to acute flaccid paralysis (AFP). It is characterized by asymmetric, flaccid paralysis with intact sensory function. Bulbar involvement can result in respiratory paralysis and death. Post-polio syndrome, occurring 15–30 years after recovery, includes muscle weakness, pain, and fatigue. 10. Laboratory Diagnosis: Diagnosis involves isolating poliovirus from stool samples of AFP patients and characterizing the virus to determine if it is vaccine-associated, VDPV, or wild poliovirus. Molecular diagnostics and sequencing are used to confirm the origin and relatedness of isolates. 11. Community-Based Surveillance (CBS): CBS involves community members reporting suspected AFP cases to designated focal points. It enhances surveillance in hard-to-reach areas and promotes community engagement. CBS can be formal (resource-intensive) or informal (low-resource). Needs assessments are conducted to determine the feasibility and efficiency of CBS in improving AFP surveillance. 12. Establishing CBS: Key steps include engaging community leaders, selecting trusted volunteers, addressing gender-related barriers, and providing training and materials. This detailed explanation provides a comprehensive understanding of the content, focusing on the technical and clinical aspects of poliovirus surveillance, vaccination, and eradication efforts.
